## Installing packages...

If you see the 'Installing package...' or 'Loading package...' message, this means that the programming language is doing some work behind the scenes to get everything working. When it's finished, it will be replaced by a 'Run Code' button.

## R code

-   R code, as most programming languages, involves manipulating data.

-   Data is usually stored as **variables** and the manipulations are usually done by applying these variables to **functions.**

-   Often, programmers will write their own functions, but in this course, we'll exclusively use existing functions, from various packages.

# Basic R operations and data types

## Numbers

You can use `+`, `-`, `*` and `/` to add, subtract, multiple, and divide, respectively.

```{webr-r}
28 + 32
```

```{webr-r}
25 - 10
```

```{webr-r}
11 * 9
```

```{webr-r}
100 / 8
```

## Multiple arithmetic actions on one line:

```{webr-r}
100 + 5 * 10
```

## Same cell block

```{webr-r}
100 * 5

50 * 4
```

## Errors..

```{webr-r}

100 * 5 50 * 4


```

## Order of operations

```{webr-r}
(100 + 5) * 10
```

Run the code above and see how it differs!

## Assigning variables

To assign a variable in R, use the command `->`. You can also use `=`, but not in all situations, so it's better to use `<-`.

To the left of this command, enter the variable name. On the right hand side, enter the value.

The following code creates a variable called `x` and assigns it the value `10`:

```{webr-r}

x <- 10
```

## Remember...

::: callout-warning
Don't forget to run the code! If you don't, the variable will not be assigned and you won't be able to use it later!
:::

## Strings

The following code will create a variable called `album_title`, and give it the value `"Dangerously in Love"`:

```{webr-r}
album_title <- "Dangerously in Love"
```

## Printing a string

```{webr-r}
print(album_title)
```

## Calculate length

```{webr-r}
nchar(album_title)
```

## Vectors

A vector of numbers looks like this:

```{webr-r}

number_vector <- c(1,2,3,4,5)


```

## Vector of strings

A vector of strings. Don't forget they need to be in inverted commas!

```{webr-r}
song_vector <- c("Crazy in Love", "Naughty Girl", "Baby Boy")
```

## Comparisons

You can compare numbers or variables using the following:

-   `==` (equals),

-   `>` (greater than),

-   `<`, (less than)

-   `!=` (not equal to).

If you put something on the left and right of these comparisons, R will check if the statement is correct and output either `TRUE` or `FALSE`:

# Comparisons with numbers.

## Equals

This checks if the value on the left is the same as the value on the right.

```{webr-r}

5 == 5


```

## Greater than

This checks if the value on the left is greater than the value on the right:

```{webr-r}

10 > 5

```

## Exercises:

-   Write a statement to check if 15 is greater than 5.


## Comparisons with strings

You can do comparisons with strings too. Note that the comparison is strict - the punctuation and capitalisation need to match exactly. Why doesn't this return `TRUE`?

```{webr-r}
"Crazy in Love" == "Crazy In Love"
```

## Comparisons with vectors

We can see if elements in a vector are greater than a given number:

```{webr-r}
v = c(1,5,4,6,7) # create a vector of numbers

v > 3 # check if the elements in the vector v are greater than 3.
```

## Comparisons with vectors

We can do the same with strings:

```{webr-r}

song_title == song_vector

```

Here, we ask R to return either TRUE or FALSE, depending on whether each element of the song_vector is the same as the song_title string.
